questions.stem: Why are fossil fuels and metallic ores classed as non-renewable resources?
options: They occur in only small amounts at a handful of sites around the world
They are destroyed completely when used, so none of their atoms remain
They can never be recycled once they have been extracted and processed
They form over millions of years, far more slowly than we extract them
questions.explanation: Non-renewable resources form over geological timescales, so they are not replenished on any timescale useful to people. Metals can in fact be recycled, but recycling does not make new ore in the ground.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the formation of coal?
options: Plant matter is buried in desert sand, oxidises in the air, then hardens into coal
Plant matter is buried by lava, melts in the heat, then cools and crystallises
Plant matter builds up in swamps, is buried as peat, then is compacted and heated
Marine plankton settles on the sea floor, is buried in mud, then is heated into coal
questions.explanation: Coal forms from land plants that accumulate in waterlogged swamps, where low oxygen slows decay and peat forms. Burial compacts and heats the peat into coal. Marine plankton is the main source of oil and gas, not coal.

questions.stem: As peat is buried more deeply over time, it changes to lignite, then bituminous coal, then anthracite. Which change occurs as coal rank increases?
options: Carbon content stays constant while the coal becomes porous
Oxygen content rises as the coal absorbs gas from the rock
Carbon content rises while water and volatile content fall
Carbon content falls while water and volatile content rise
questions.explanation: Increasing heat and pressure drive off water and volatile compounds, so higher-rank coal is richer in carbon and releases more energy per tonne. Anthracite is the highest-rank coal.

questions.stem: Oil and natural gas mainly form from:
options: remains of large land animals preserved in desert sands and dunes
microscopic marine organisms buried in fine sediment without oxygen
woody land plants buried in freshwater swamps and compressed to peat
carbon dioxide from volcanoes that reacts with water deep underground
questions.explanation: Most petroleum comes from plankton and algae that settled in oxygen-poor water and were buried in mud, later becoming organic-rich shale. Woody land plants in swamps mainly form coal.

questions.stem: Organic matter in a buried shale is heated as burial depth increases. Why is oil generated mainly within a limited depth range called the oil window?
options: Above this range oxygen burns the oil, and below it bacteria consume the oil
Only within this range is there enough water to dissolve the kerogen into oil
Too little heat leaves the kerogen unaltered, while too much breaks oil into gas
Too little pressure keeps oil liquid, while too much turns the oil into coal seams
questions.explanation: Kerogen needs enough heat to break down into liquid hydrocarbons. At greater depth and higher temperature, oil molecules crack into smaller gas molecules. Bacteria cannot survive the high temperatures at depth, so they do not destroy oil below the window.

questions.stem: For a commercial gas field to form, which combination of rocks is needed?
options: An organic-rich source rock, an impermeable reservoir rock and a porous permeable seal
A granite source rock, a porous permeable reservoir rock and a fractured limestone seal
A porous source rock, an impermeable reservoir rock and a permeable sandstone seal
An organic-rich source rock, a porous permeable reservoir rock and an impermeable seal
questions.explanation: Gas forms in an organic-rich source rock, migrates into a reservoir rock whose connected pores can hold and transmit it, and is held there by an impermeable seal or cap rock. Without a seal the gas escapes to the surface.

questions.stem: In an anticline trap, why does gas collect at the crest of the fold?
options: The crest is the hottest part of the fold, so gas is generated right there
Gas dissolves in the cap rock at the crest, where that rock is most porous
Gas is less dense than water and oil, so it rises until the seal stops it
Gas is denser than water and oil, so it is pushed into the fold's crest
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons are buoyant and migrate upward through the reservoir rock. In an arch-shaped anticline they rise to the highest point and are held beneath the impermeable cap rock, with gas above oil above water.

questions.stem: The Pilbara's great iron ore deposits are hosted in banded iron formations. How did these formations originally form?
options: Iron weathered from granite on land was washed into rivers and deposited as sandbars
Dissolved iron in ancient seawater reacted with oxygen and settled out as iron oxide layers
Iron-rich lava erupted onto the ancient sea floor and cooled into alternating layers of basalt
Iron meteorites struck the early Earth and were buried in thick layers of marine mud
questions.explanation: Banded iron formations are chemical sedimentary rocks. Oxygen released by photosynthesising microbes reacted with dissolved iron in the oceans, and insoluble iron oxides settled on the sea floor in layers alternating with silica-rich chert.

questions.stem: Banded iron formation typically contains about 30% iron, but the high-grade Pilbara ores contain about 60%. Which process mainly upgraded the ore?
options: Fluids leached silica out of the formation, leaving iron oxides concentrated behind
Magma injected extra iron into the formation, filling its pores with fresh magnetite
Compaction squeezed water out of the formation, doubling its iron content by mass
Bacteria converted the silica into iron oxide, raising the proportion of iron
questions.explanation: Later fluids, both deep hydrothermal fluids and descending groundwater, dissolved the silica-rich chert bands and replaced them with iron oxides. Removing silica concentrates the iron, roughly doubling the grade.

questions.stem: Kambalda nickel sulfide deposits occur at the base of ultramafic lava flows in ancient greenstone belts. Which process concentrated the nickel?
options: Weathering at the surface removed the lava and left nickel in residual soils
Nickel-rich mud settled in a lake and was later buried beneath lava flows
Dense sulfide liquid separated from the magma and sank to the base of the flow
Seawater circulating through the cooled lava dissolved nickel and carried it up
questions.explanation: These are magmatic deposits. Sulfide liquid does not mix with silicate magma, and being denser it collects at the base of the flow, taking nickel, copper and iron with it. Weathering concentrates nickel in a different type, the lateritic deposits.

questions.stem: Lateritic nickel deposits form near the surface over ultramafic rocks. Which process forms them?
options: Deep chemical weathering in a warm, wet climate that concentrated nickel in the regolith
Separation of dense sulfide liquid from the magma and its settling at the base of hot ultramafic lava flows
Hydrothermal fluids rising along deep faults and depositing nickel in quartz veins
Metamorphism of buried nickel-rich shale under high temperature and pressure
questions.explanation: Prolonged weathering dissolves and removes the more soluble elements from ultramafic rock, leaving less mobile nickel concentrated in the weathered profile. Magmatic sulfide separation forms a different type of nickel deposit.

questions.stem: An exploration company is searching Western Australia for komatiite-hosted nickel sulfides. Where should it focus?
options: Limestone plateaus with extensive caves and karst landforms
Archean greenstone belts containing ultramafic volcanic rocks
Young sedimentary basins containing thick sequences of coal seams
Coastal dune systems with heavy mineral sands along beaches
questions.explanation: Komatiites are ultramafic lavas erupted mainly in the Archean, and they are preserved in greenstone belts such as those of the Yilgarn Craton. Location of a resource depends on its geological setting, so explorers target rocks that can host it.

questions.stem: The gold deposits of the Kalgoorlie region formed mainly by:
options: plant material concentrating gold in swamps that later hardened into coal
hot fluids moving along faults and shear zones and depositing gold in quartz veins
gold settling from seawater onto the ocean floor with layers of banded iron
gold crystallising directly from cooling granite magma as large nuggets deep underground
questions.explanation: Kalgoorlie's lode gold is hydrothermal. Hot fluids, mobilised during deformation and metamorphism, travelled along faults and shear zones and deposited gold with quartz and sulfide minerals where conditions changed.

questions.stem: Prospectors find gold nuggets concentrated in creek-bed gravels and at the bends of old river channels. Why does gold accumulate there?
options: Gold is magnetic, so it is drawn toward iron-rich gravels at the river bends
Gold is very dense, so it settles out where water slows while lighter grains move on
Gold is chemically reactive, so it precipitates when creek water becomes saturated
Gold is very light, so it floats downstream until trapped by the creek's gravel bars
questions.explanation: These are placer deposits, formed by sedimentary processes. Gold weathered from lodes is far denser than quartz sand, so it drops out wherever the current slows. Gold is unreactive and not magnetic.

questions.stem: Which pairing of resource and forming process is correct?
options: Coal: magmatic; banded iron formation: hydrothermal
Lode gold: sedimentary; coal: magmatic
Placer gold: sedimentary; nickel sulfide: magmatic
Placer gold: hydrothermal; nickel sulfide: sedimentary
questions.explanation: Placer gold is concentrated by flowing water, a sedimentary process, and nickel sulfides separate from ultramafic magma. Lode gold is hydrothermal, and coal and banded iron formations are sedimentary.

questions.stem: Why are hydrothermal ore deposits often found along faults?
options: Faults block all groundwater flow, so metals cannot escape the nearby rock
Faults provide permeable pathways that focus the flow of hot, mineral-rich fluids
Faults generate enough heat by friction to melt the surrounding rock directly into ore
Faults trap meteorites, which supply the metals found in hydrothermal veins
questions.explanation: Broken rock in fault and shear zones lets fluids flow much more easily than through intact rock. Metals carried in solution are deposited where the fluid cools, reacts with wall rock or loses pressure.

questions.stem: Which geophysical survey would best detect a buried, magnetite-rich banded iron formation?
options: A seismic survey
A stream sediment survey
A magnetic survey
A radiometric survey
questions.explanation: Magnetite is strongly magnetic, so a magnetite-rich unit produces a clear anomaly in a magnetic survey, often flown from aircraft. Radiometric surveys detect gamma rays from potassium, uranium and thorium, not magnetite.

questions.stem: Nickel sulfide ore conducts electricity much better than the rocks around it. Which method takes advantage of this?
options: Radiometric surveys, which detect gamma rays given off by electrically conductive minerals
Seismic surveys, which detect sound waves produced by electric currents in ore bodies
Electromagnetic surveys, which induce currents in conductive bodies and measure the response
Gravity surveys, which measure small variations in the electrical charge of buried rocks
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic surveys use electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field induces currents in conductors, and their secondary field is measured. Gravity surveys measure density, not electrical properties.

questions.stem: Why are seismic reflection surveys widely used in petroleum exploration?
options: They sample the chemistry of the soil to show which rocks hold oil at depth
They image rock layers and structures, such as anticlines and faults, that can trap oil and gas
They detect the magnetic field of oil directly, showing exactly how much oil each reservoir holds
They measure gamma rays given off by gas, showing the depth of each gas reservoir
questions.explanation: Sound waves reflect off boundaries between rock layers, producing an image of subsurface structure. This locates possible traps, but only drilling shows whether they actually contain oil or gas.

questions.stem: A gravity survey over a region shows a strong positive anomaly. What could this indicate?
options: A body of rock less dense than its surroundings, such as a thick salt dome
A body of rock more radioactive than its surroundings, such as uranium ore
A body of rock more magnetic than its surroundings but no denser than the rock around it
A body of rock denser than its surroundings, such as massive sulfide or iron ore
questions.explanation: Gravity surveys detect differences in density. Dense ore bodies give a positive anomaly, while low-density bodies such as salt or thick sedimentary basins give negative anomalies.

questions.stem: A geologist collects soil samples on a grid and finds unusually high nickel and copper concentrations over one area. How should this be interpreted?
options: It shows the metals washed in from elsewhere, so the bedrock below must be barren
It is a geochemical anomaly that may lie above mineralisation and should be drill-tested
It proves an economic ore body lies beneath, so mining can begin without drilling
It shows contamination from the sampling equipment, so the whole area should now be ignored
questions.explanation: Geochemical surveys find anomalies that point to possible mineralisation, but they cannot show the grade, size or depth of a deposit. Drilling is needed to test the target.

questions.stem: How do satellite-based spectrometers help geologists find mineral deposits?
options: Minerals emit radio waves when struck by sunlight, so satellites can measure ore tonnage
Satellites measure rock density directly, so ore bodies appear as dark patches in images
Minerals reflect sunlight at characteristic wavelengths, so alteration minerals can be mapped
Satellite sensors detect gamma rays from ore hundreds of metres beneath the surface
questions.explanation: Each mineral absorbs and reflects light at particular wavelengths. Spectral images can map clays, iron oxides and other alteration minerals at the surface, which can surround hidden deposits. They only sense the surface.

questions.stem: Aerial photographs are useful in the early stages of exploration mainly because they:
options: measure the metal grade of buried ore bodies to within a fraction of a per cent from the air
detect electrical conductors hundreds of metres below the surface directly
replace the need for drilling to confirm the size and grade of a deposit
reveal regional structures, outcrops and drainage patterns over large areas quickly
questions.explanation: Aerial photographs give a broad, cheap view of outcrop, faults, folds and drainage, helping geologists map and choose areas for detailed work. They give no information about grade at depth.

questions.stem: Why is drilling still needed after geophysical and geochemical surveys have identified a target?
options: Only drill samples can confirm the grade, thickness and extent of the mineralisation
Drilling is cheaper than remote sensing, so it replaces the earlier survey results
Drill holes create the magnetic anomalies that later geophysical surveys detect
Drilling is required only to supply water for the processing plant on site
questions.explanation: Surveys show where a deposit may be, but only samples of the rock itself, from drill core or chips, show how much metal it contains and how far it extends. Drilling is expensive, which is why it comes last.

questions.stem: Which order of exploration methods best balances cost against detail?
options: Soil sampling, then drilling, then aerial surveys to find the region of interest
Ground geophysics everywhere, then satellite images, then a final aerial survey
Satellite and aerial surveys, then ground geophysics and soil sampling, then drilling
Drilling on a close grid across the whole region, then ground geophysics, then satellite surveys
questions.explanation: Exploration narrows down from cheap regional methods covering large areas, to more detailed ground methods over smaller targets, to costly drilling of the best targets.

questions.stem: Improvements in airborne geophysics and satellite spectroscopy over recent decades have mainly:
options: removed the need for drilling, since deposits can now be measured from the air
sped up the rate at which ore deposits form by detecting them at an early stage
lowered the value of every deposit by making them all equally easy to find
raised the rate of discovery and improved estimates of deposit size before mining
questions.explanation: Coupled geophysical methods and remote sensing let companies cover large areas quickly and target drilling better, so more resources are identified and their size and value estimated before extraction.

questions.stem: Gold prospect A has 1 million tonnes of ore at 8 g/t, beside a highway and power line. Prospect B has 4 million tonnes at 2 g/t in a remote area with no infrastructure. Which statement is best?
options: Both hold 8 t of gold, so their development costs and value must be identical
Both hold 8 t of gold, but A is likely cheaper to develop because of its grade and location
B holds four times as much gold as A, so B is clearly the better prospect to develop first
A holds four times as much gold as B, so B should be abandoned without further work
questions.explanation: 1 000 000 t × 8 g/t and 4 000 000 t × 2 g/t both equal 8 000 000 g, or 8 t. A needs only a quarter of the rock mined and processed for the same gold, and it is close to infrastructure.

questions.stem: An iron ore deposit contains 200 million tonnes of ore at 60% iron. How much iron does it contain?
options: 60 million tonnes
200 million tonnes
333 million tonnes
120 million tonnes
questions.explanation: Contained metal equals tonnage × grade: 200 million t × 0.60 = 120 million t of iron. Dividing by 0.60 instead gives 333 million t, which is more than the ore itself.

questions.stem: An open-cut mine removes 18 million tonnes of waste rock to extract 6 million tonnes of ore. Which statement about its strip ratio is correct?
options: It is 3 : 1, and more waste per tonne of ore lowers costs because waste is sold
It is 1 : 3, and the ratio affects only ore grade, not costs or waste dumps
It is 3 : 1, and more waste per tonne of ore raises costs and the area of waste dumps
It is 1 : 3, and less waste per tonne of ore lowers costs and the area of waste dumps
questions.explanation: Strip ratio is waste to ore: 18 : 6 = 3 : 1. Every tonne of waste must be blasted, hauled and stored, so a higher ratio means higher costs and larger waste dumps to rehabilitate.

questions.stem: Acid mine drainage forms when:
options: sulfide minerals such as pyrite in exposed rock react with oxygen and water
carbonate minerals such as calcite in waste rock dissolve in falling rain
rain in open pits absorbs nitrogen from the air and forms nitric acid
iron oxides in banded iron formation react with salt from groundwater
questions.explanation: Mining exposes sulfides to air and water, and their oxidation produces sulfuric acid. Carbonate minerals do the opposite: they neutralise acid, which is why limestone is used to treat acid drainage.

questions.stem: Why is acid drainage from a sulfide-rich waste dump harmful to a nearby creek?
options: The acid raises the pH of the creek, making the water too alkaline for fish to survive
The acid adds nutrients that cause algal blooms but has no direct toxic effect
The acid hardens the creek bed, so water can no longer soak into the ground
The low pH dissolves toxic metals, and together they harm aquatic life downstream
questions.explanation: Acid water lowers the pH and dissolves metals such as aluminium, copper and zinc from rock, and both the acidity and the metals are toxic to aquatic organisms. Acid lowers pH rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Open pits below the water table in the Pilbara must be dewatered by pumping out groundwater. Which is a likely environmental effect?
options: A cone of depression lowers the water table, stressing groundwater-dependent plants and pools
The water table rises around the pit, waterlogging the soil and drowning nearby vegetation
Groundwater salinity drops to zero, so the aquifer becomes drinkable without any treatment
Pumping draws water in from the nearest river, turning the pit into a permanent wetland
questions.explanation: Pumping draws down the water table around the pit in a cone of depression. Springs, pools and deep-rooted trees that rely on groundwater can be stressed or lost. Extraction of resources affects hydrologic systems and the biota that depend on them.

questions.stem: Surplus water from dewatering is sometimes released into an ephemeral Pilbara creek that normally flows only after rain. Why can this harm the creek ecosystem?
options: Groundwater always contains cyanide, so it kills every organism downstream within hours
Released water carries sediment uphill, burying the creek's headwaters in fine silt
Constant flow changes a system adapted to drying, altering which plants and animals survive
Extra water lowers the water table along the creek, drying out the river red gums on its banks
questions.explanation: Organisms of ephemeral creeks are adapted to cycles of flow and drying. Permanent flow favours different species, can waterlog trees and change channel shape. Adding water raises, not lowers, the local water table.

questions.stem: Gold is commonly extracted from ore using cyanide solutions. Which environmental control is most important at the tailings storage facility?
options: Adding fertiliser to the tailings so that plants take up the cyanide harmlessly
Diluting tailings with creek water so the cyanide flows away from the site quickly
Containing tailings and keeping cyanide low so wildlife drinking there is not poisoned
Spreading tailings over nearby bushland so the cyanide breaks down in sunlight
questions.explanation: Birds and other animals are attracted to water at tailings facilities, so cyanide concentrations must be kept below toxic levels and tailings contained to stop seepage. Spreading or diluting tailings spreads the contamination.

questions.stem: Before an exploration crew enters the jarrah forest, its vehicles are washed down to remove soil. Why?
options: To stop native seeds being carried out of the forest on the vehicles' tyres
To avoid spreading soil carrying the Phytophthora dieback pathogen into healthy forest
To avoid fuel and oil spills from the vehicles contaminating the groundwater beneath the forest
To remove dust that would interfere with the magnetic survey instruments
questions.explanation: Phytophthora dieback is spread in infected soil and kills many jarrah forest plants. Clean-down and hygiene procedures are an environmental consideration even at the exploration stage, before any mining begins.

questions.stem: Which step is part of rehabilitating a mine site when it closes?
options: Planting one fast-growing exotic species to cover the site as quickly as possible
Removing all remaining topsoil from the site so weeds cannot grow on the dumps
Reshaping waste dumps, spreading stored topsoil and replanting local native species
Leaving waste dumps as they are, since bare slopes are stable and do not erode
questions.explanation: Decommissioning aims to leave a safe, stable, non-polluting landform that supports a self-sustaining ecosystem. Steep bare dumps erode, and a single exotic species does not restore the original ecosystem.

questions.stem: Why is topsoil stripped and stockpiled separately before mining, then returned as soon as possible?
options: It is sterile and heavy, so returning it quickly stops the waste dumps blowing away
It is toxic to native plants, so it is buried deep beneath the waste dump for safety
It holds the seed bank, nutrients and soil organisms needed to revegetate, which decline in storage
It contains most of the valuable ore, so it must be processed separately from the waste rock first
questions.explanation: Topsoil is the most biologically active part of the soil. Its seeds, microbes and fungi die off the longer it sits in a stockpile, so direct return gives the best revegetation.

questions.stem: After mining ends, a pit dug below the water table fills with groundwater to form a pit lake in an arid region. Over decades the lake becomes steadily more saline. What is the best explanation?
options: Evaporation from the lake surface removes water but leaves the dissolved salts behind
Rain falling on the lake adds salt, since rainwater is saltier than the groundwater
The pit walls absorb fresh water, leaving only the saltiest water in the lake
Algae growing in the lake produce salt chemically once the pit has filled
questions.explanation: Where evaporation greatly exceeds rainfall, water leaves the lake as vapour while salts stay behind and concentrate. This is why pit lakes need long-term monitoring as part of closure planning.

questions.stem: Before a new mine is approved, consultation and negotiation with local and Indigenous communities are required mainly to:
options: assess the environmental, cultural and community impacts and costs of removing the resource
decide the exact ore grade, since only community members may analyse the drill samples
replace the need for any environmental impact assessment by government agencies
confirm the geological setting of the deposit from community records of rock types
questions.explanation: Whether and how to extract a resource depends on its value, location and volume, and also on its impacts on the environment and on the people connected to the land. Consultation is part of assessing those impacts, alongside formal environmental assessment.

questions.stem: A Pilbara mine plans to dewater an aquifer that feeds a permanent spring pool used by fish and waterbirds. Which monitoring would best show the effect of mining on this ecosystem?
options: Bore water levels, spring flow and pool biota, surveyed before and during mining
Ore grade in drill core, collected before and during mining from the pit floor and walls
Rainfall at the mine site only, recorded once when mining first begins
Dust settling on leaves near the haul roads, measured after mining ends
questions.explanation: Baseline data from before mining, compared with data during mining, shows whether water levels, flow and the dependent organisms have changed. The other measures do not link the dewatering to the spring ecosystem.
